words: light source; reflect; transmit; absorb; refract; ray; transparent; translucent; opaque; receptor
notes: Base unit 6.1 (one-way mirror). Light travels from a source in straight lines until it meets a material; there it is reflected, transmitted or (with s6-insulator-design) absorbed, depending on the material, and its path bends where it crosses from one transparent material into another (air to water, air to glass). We see an object only when light from it enters the eye, so a one-way mirror works because far more light reaches one side than the other. Students draw and revise ray diagrams (the light-ray model, a new shared name: the ray model of light paths, which the wave-model name does not cover) and test them with flashlights, mirrors and films. Owns MS-PS4-2 by exception: the base text completes this PE across 6.1, 6.2, 8.2 and 8.4, but every PE of 6.1 is completed in grade 8, and a row must name a standard. The light half of the PE (reflect, absorb, transmit, bend) is finished in grade 6; s8-wave-amplitude-energy adds the mechanical-wave half (sound in a medium) and s8-earth-sun-moon adds light crossing empty space and color bending by different amounts. Also starts MS-LS1-8 (owned by s8-senses-brain): the eye has receptors that respond to light and send signals to the brain. Boundary: qualitative only; no wave equations, no lens formulas. Teacher note: no laser pointers into eyes; flashlights or low-power class 2 lasers only, beam kept below eye level.

words: particle; kinetic energy; temperature; thermal energy; energy transfer; mass; variable; control
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (temperature against time as two quantities that change together)
notes: Base unit 6.2 (double-walled cup). Matter is made of particles always in motion; temperature measures the average kinetic energy of those particles, and energy moves from the warmer sample to the cooler one through collisions until they match. Students plan and run fair tests of how the energy transferred depends on the type of matter, the mass and the temperature change (ice melting in different amounts of water; equal masses of different materials cooling), choosing what to vary, hold steady and measure, then graph temperature against time. Heat is used in its science sense, energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Also starts MS-PS3-5 (owned by s8-energy-transfer-argument): when particles speed up or slow down, energy has been transferred. Boundary: no calculation of the total energy transferred. Teacher note: hot water no hotter than a tap or kettle-cooled 60 C, kept by the teacher; spills wiped at once.

words: conduction; convection; radiation; insulator; conductor; criteria; constraints; prototype; system; boundary
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.5 (summarize repeated trial data with a measure of center)
notes: Base unit 6.2. Students apply what they found about particle collisions, moving air or water carrying energy, and light being absorbed (the absorbed part of MS-PS4-2) to design, build and test a cup or container that keeps a drink cold longest, against criteria (temperature change over a set time) and constraints (cost, materials, size). Each design is drawn as a system with a boundary, with arrows for energy moving in or out. Students test, compare and revise. Also starts MS-ETS1-4 (owned by s7-design-optimize): a model is used to predict and test design changes before building. Boundary: no calculation of energy transferred. Teacher note: as for s6-particle-temperature; no glass containers for student-built designs.

words: solid; liquid; gas; melting; freezing; evaporation; condensation; state; pure substance
cross_subject: math:6.NS.C.5 (temperatures below zero as negative numbers)
notes: Base unit 6.3 (hail falling on warm days). Particle drawings of solids (close, vibrating in place), liquids (touching, sliding past) and gases (far apart, colliding) are used to predict what happens when thermal energy is added or removed: the particles speed up or slow down until the substance changes state, and the same particles remain. Students explain condensation on a cold can and freezing water drops high in a storm cloud. Completes MS-PS1-4, which s6-particle-temperature started. Examples: water, carbon dioxide (dry ice, teacher handled), helium. Boundary: qualitative molecular models; no latent heat values. Teacher note: dry ice only with gloves and tongs by the teacher, never sealed in a container.

words: water cycle; evaporation; condensation; precipitation; runoff; groundwater; humidity; gravity
notes: Base unit 6.3. Water moves through ocean, air, land, ice and living things on many paths, changing state as it goes. Energy from the sun drives evaporation and lifts water vapor; gravity pulls precipitation, runoff and groundwater downhill. Students build a model from their particle and energy ideas and use it to trace how water reaches a hailstorm and returns to the ground. Introduces the water-cycle model at middle school depth (if an earlier band already hands it on, it becomes a carry). Boundary: latent heat is not treated with numbers.

words: air mass; air pressure; front; humidity; wind; forecast; probability; weather
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (pressure and temperature against time)
notes: Base unit 6.3. Air flows from high pressure to low pressure; where warm, moist air rises and cools, clouds and storms form, and where different air masses meet (a front) the weather can change suddenly. Students collect or are given temperature, pressure, humidity and wind data and weather maps, find patterns, and say what weather is likely at a place, as a range of chances, not a certainty. Boundary: students are not asked to recall cloud names or weather-map symbols.

words: climate; latitude; altitude; prevailing wind; ocean current; uneven heating; rotation
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-mena-maps (latitude bands on a map)
notes: Base unit 6.3, second anchor (regional rain patterns). Climate is the long-run pattern of weather. Sunlight heats the Earth unevenly by latitude (sunlight strike the poles at a low angle, reusing the earth-sun-moon model from earlier grades), so air and ocean water circulate in large loops; the Earth's rotation turns winds and currents into steady patterns (prevailing winds, ocean currents carrying warm water toward the poles). With mountains, distance from the ocean and altitude, these explain why regions have the climates they do. Boundary: the Coriolis effect is named and its result used; its dynamics are not taught.

words: rock cycle; igneous; sedimentary; metamorphic; weathering; erosion; deposition; magma; crystallization
notes: Base unit 6.4 (Mount Everest rising). Earth materials cycle: melting, crystallization, weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction and deformation turn rocks from one kind into another. Energy from the Earth's hot interior drives melting and uplift; energy from the sun drives the water and wind that weather and carry rock. Students build the rock-cycle model and trace how marine rock ends up near the top of a mountain. Boundary: no naming of minerals.

words: uplift; landslide; glacier; time scale; gradual; catastrophic; landform
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3b (rates such as millimeters per year)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Processes shape the surface at very different speeds and sizes: plates move a few centimeters a year and mountains rise over millions of years, while a landslide or eruption changes a slope in minutes. Students compare rates and explain a landform, choosing a local one where possible, as the sum of slow change punctuated by sudden events. The reasoning that grows is scale: a tiny rate over a huge time makes a huge change.

words: plate; plate tectonics; continent; seafloor; ridge; trench; fossil; evidence
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3b (spreading rate as distance per year)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Students analyze maps of matching fossils and rocks across oceans, the fit of continental shelves, and the ridges and trenches on the seafloor, and argue that the plates have moved and are still moving. They build the plate model (plates moving apart, together and past each other) and use it to explain mountains such as the Himalaya. Boundary: magnetic striping of the seafloor is not assessed.

words: rock layer; strata; relative age; geologic time scale; fossil; superposition; billion
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-timeline-deep-time (scaled timeline of deep time)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Rock layers and the fossils in them are read in order (lower layers formed first unless the rocks were disturbed) to put events in sequence; the geologic time scale organizes the Earth's 4.6-billion-year history, from the formation of the Earth and the earliest life to the last ice age. Students build a scaled timeline and place mountain building, extinctions and eruptions on it. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5): the age of the Earth is stated plainly. Boundary: no recall of the names of periods or epochs.

words: natural hazard; earthquake; tsunami; forecast; mitigate; warning system; magnitude; frequency
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.4 (histograms of magnitudes and frequencies)
notes: Base unit 6.5 (the 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami). Students map where and how often earthquakes, eruptions, tsunamis and storms happen, and use the plate model to explain the pattern. Some hazards give warning signs that allow forecasts (eruptions, hurricanes); earthquakes do not yet. They use the data to judge which technologies reduce harm (sea walls, warning buoys, evacuation routes, building design). Also starts MS-ETS1-1 (owned by s7-define-design-problem) and MS-ETS1-2 (owned by s8-design-evaluate): students state criteria and constraints for a tsunami-safety solution and compare two options. Teacher note: loss of life is discussed with care; some students may have lived through a disaster, so the unit uses data and design, not graphic images, and gives a way to step out.

words: signal; analog; digital; encode; transmit; noise; reliable
cross_subject: ela:RI.6.7 (integrate information from text, images and video)
notes: Base unit 6.5, lesson added in 2022 (alert systems). Waves can carry information. Students read and watch how warning systems changed from sirens and analog radio to digital alerts, and support the claim that digital signals are more reliable: a pattern of on and off pulses can be copied and re-sent without the small errors that build up in an analog signal. Boundary: no binary counting and no workings of any particular device. The wave-model carried here is the pulse or wave as a carrier of a pattern; amplitude and energy wait for s8-wave-amplitude-energy.

words: cell; organism; unicellular; multicellular; microscope; tissue; organ; cell membrane; cell wall; nerve
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.1 (magnification as a ratio)
notes: Base unit 6.6 (a student breaks two bones in his foot). Students use microscopes and images to gather evidence that all living things are made of cells, one or many, and that cells tell living from non-living things. Also starts three PEs completed later: MS-LS1-2 (cell membrane and cell wall control what enters and leaves; owned by s8-cell-parts-function), MS-LS1-3 (cells form tissues and organs that work together in healing: skeletal, muscular, circulatory, nervous; owned by s7-body-systems-food) and MS-LS1-8 (nerve cells carry signals from receptors to the brain, felt as touch and pain; owned by s8-senses-brain). Teacher note: no human body fluids or cheek-cell swabs; prepared slides, plant and pond samples; glass slides and coverslips handled by the edges; the injury case is described without graphic images.

words: substance; property; atom; molecule; chemical reaction; reactant; product; conservation of matter; mass
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.1 (ratios of atoms in a molecule)
notes: Base unit 7.1 (a bath bomb fizzing away). Each pure substance has properties (density, melting point, solubility, odor, flammability) that identify it; substances are made of atoms joined into molecules; in a chemical reaction the atoms of the starting substances regroup into new molecules with new properties, and the number of each kind of atom stays the same, so mass is conserved (shown by weighing a reaction in a closed bag). Starts MS-PS1-1 and MS-PS1-2, which s7-food-molecules completes, and MS-LS1-8 (smell receptors respond to molecules; owned by s8-senses-brain). Boundary: no atomic masses, no balancing of symbolic equations, no bonding forces. Teacher note: eye protection for all mixing; citric acid and baking soda only; no tasting; closed bags vented away from faces.

words: release energy; absorb energy; exothermic; endothermic; concentration; surroundings
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (temperature against time for each reaction)
notes: Base unit 7.2 (the flameless heater in a field ration). Some reactions release energy to their surroundings and some take it in; the temperature of the system tells which. Students explain this with the particle model and design, test and modify a homemade heater or cold pack, varying the type and amount of substance. Boundary: criteria limited to amount, time and temperature. Teacher note: eye protection and gloves; calcium chloride and ammonium chloride only, in small amounts, never tasted; the field-ration heater is a teacher demonstration in a ventilated room, since it gives off hydrogen and gets very hot.

words: optimize; iterate; model; test; trade-off; variable
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.2a (is the temperature change proportional to the amount used)
notes: Base unit 7.2. Students use a model (a small-scale test, a table of earlier results, a simple simulation) to generate data, change one variable at a time, and modify the heater design step by step toward the best result within the constraints. Completes MS-ETS1-4, started in s6-insulator-design. Also builds MS-ETS1-2 and MS-ETS1-3, owned by grade 8 rows, by comparing designs against criteria and combining the best features. Teacher note: as for s7-reaction-energy.

words: carbohydrate; starch; sugar; protein; fat; extended structure; digestion; indicator
notes: Base unit 7.3 (a student with stomach pain and weight loss). Completes MS-PS1-1 and MS-PS1-2, started in s7-reactions-atoms. Food is made of large molecules (starch, proteins, fats) with repeating subunits, and simple molecules (sugars, water); students model molecules of very different sizes (a scale idea: a starch molecule holds thousands of atoms, a water molecule three) and extended structures (a salt crystal, starch). They read data on properties before and after digestion (starch tests, sugar tests) to decide whether a chemical reaction has happened: large molecules are broken into smaller ones the body can use. Boundary: properties limited to density, melting and boiling point, solubility, flammability and odor; no valence electrons or full atom-by-atom drawings of large molecules. Teacher note: indicator solutions (iodine, glucose strips) with eye protection; no tasting; the case is about a real health condition, discussed without asking students about their own.

words: subsystem; digestive system; circulatory system; respiratory system; excretory system; tissue; organ
cross_subject: ela:W.7.1 (written argument with evidence)
notes: Base unit 7.3. Completes MS-LS1-3, started in s6-cells-body-systems. Students argue from evidence how the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, excretory and muscular systems work together to get food molecules and oxygen to every cell and take wastes away, and what goes wrong when one part (the small intestine lining) is damaged. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. Boundary: limited to these six systems with the nervous system; no mechanism of one system studied alone.

words: cellular respiration; glucose; oxygen; carbon dioxide; energy release; growth; repair
notes: Base unit 7.3. Inside cells, food molecules are broken apart and rebuilt: some atoms are rearranged into new molecules the body uses to grow and repair, and some molecules react with oxygen, releasing energy and giving off carbon dioxide and water. Students model the matter moving through the body and the energy released. Boundary: no details of the chemical reactions of respiration; no named intermediate molecules.

words: photosynthesis; chloroplast; producer; glucose; carbon dioxide; light energy; sap
cross_subject: ela:W.7.2 (written scientific explanation)
notes: Base unit 7.4 (where maple syrup and breakfast foods come from). Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and, using light energy in their chloroplasts, rearrange the atoms into sugars and give off oxygen; most of a tree's mass comes from the air. Students explain from evidence (plant mass data, gas measurements) how photosynthesis moves matter and energy into organisms. Starts the 7.4 part of MS-LS1-2 (chloroplasts and mitochondria; owned by s8-cell-parts-function). Boundary: no biochemical steps of photosynthesis. Teacher note: tasting of syrup or sap only under the school's food policy and with allergy checks.

words: natural resource; synthetic; material; process; impact; society
cross_subject: ela:W.7.8 (gather information from several sources)
notes: Base unit 7.4. Natural resources (plants, oil, minerals) are changed by chemical processes into synthetic materials such as plastics, medicines, fuels and sweeteners. Students gather and weigh information on one material: what it is made from, what reaction changes it, and how it helps and harms people and places. Boundary: qualitative only.

words: ecosystem; producer; consumer; decomposer; food web; matter cycle; energy flow; system boundary
notes: Base unit 7.4. Matter cycles among producers, consumers, decomposers, air, water and soil and is conserved; energy flows in from the sun and out as heat and is not recycled. Students draw a system boundary around an ecosystem (a maple forest) and model where the atoms go and where the energy goes, including decomposers breaking down dead matter. Boundary: no chemical equations for the processes.

words: population; resource; limiting factor; abundant; scarce; carrying capacity
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (population against time)
notes: Base unit 7.5 (rainforest cleared for palm oil and the animals that live there). Students analyze population data to show that when food, water, space or shelter is plentiful, organisms grow and populations rise, and when it is scarce they fall. The reasoning grows from one organism to a whole population over time.

words: competition; predation; mutualism; parasitism; interaction; abiotic; biotic
notes: Base unit 7.5. The same kinds of interactions (competition, predator and prey, mutually beneficial partners) recur across very different ecosystems. Students use these patterns to predict what will happen to one population when another changes, in an ecosystem they have not studied.

words: disruption; habitat loss; invasive species; biodiversity; argument
cross_subject: ela:W.7.1 (written argument with evidence)
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students argue from data that a change to the physical or living parts of an ecosystem (clearing, drought, a new species) changes its populations, and judge whether another group's evidence supports its claim.

words: biodiversity; ecosystem service; trade-off; stakeholder; sustainable
cross_subject: ela:RI.7.8 (judge whether evidence supports a claim)
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students compare solutions that keep biodiversity and ecosystem services (clean water, soil, pollination) while meeting people's needs, such as farming methods and protected corridors, weighing scientific, economic and social constraints. Starts MS-ESS3-3 (human impacts; owned by s7-human-impact-design).

words: criteria; constraints; precise; impact; stakeholder
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students define a design problem precisely enough to solve it: the need, measurable criteria for success, and constraints, including science limits and possible harm to people and the environment. Completes MS-ETS1-1, started in s6-hazard-forecast.

words: natural resource; mineral; ore; fossil fuel; groundwater; renewable; non-renewable; uneven distribution
notes: Base unit 7.6 (changing rain and water supply). Minerals, fossil fuels and groundwater are found where past and present geologic processes put them: oil where marine life was buried, metal ores near old volcanic zones, groundwater in porous rock, soil where rock weathers. Most are limited and non-renewable in a human lifetime, and people are using them up. Students explain a local or regional resource from the rock-cycle and plate models.

words: global temperature; greenhouse gas; carbon dioxide; methane; fossil fuel; climate change; correlation; cause
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.5 (summarize temperature records)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Students ask questions of temperature records, gas levels and human activity data to find what has raised the global temperature over the past century, separating correlation from cause, and link warmer air holding more water to the changing rain they started from. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5): human activities, chiefly burning fossil fuels, are the main cause; natural factors (sunlight, volcanoes) are weighed and found smaller.

words: per capita; consumption; population growth; impact; rate
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent increase in population and use)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Students argue from data that as human population and use per person of water, food, minerals and energy rise, the effects on Earth systems grow unless technologies and choices change. Science describes the consequences; it does not decide what a society should do.

words: monitor; minimize; human impact; water use; land use; pollution; solution
cross_subject: ela:W.7.7 (short research project)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Completes MS-ESS3-3, started in s7-biodiversity-solutions. Students design a method to monitor and reduce one human impact on water in their community (rain gardens, permeable paving, water reuse) and evaluate it against criteria and constraints. Teacher note: community water problems can touch families directly; keep the focus on solutions and on data, not blame.

words: force; collision; interaction; Newton's third law; equal; opposite; direction
cross_subject: math:7.NS.A.1 (opposite directions as positive and negative)
notes: Base unit 8.1 (a dropped phone that cracks or does not). In a collision, each object pushes on the other with a force of the same size in the opposite direction. Students draw force diagrams for collisions and apply this to design packaging or a case that protects an object. Starts MS-PS2-2, MS-PS3-1 and MS-PS3-5, completed in 8.3 rows, and MS-LS1-8 (touch and pressure receptors; owned by s8-senses-brain). Boundary: one dimension, vertical or horizontal. Teacher note: drop tests from low heights onto soft surfaces, eggs or phones replaced by safe stand-ins; eye protection when anything may break.

words: decision matrix; systematic; evaluate; weigh; criteria; constraints
cross_subject: math:6.EE.A.2c (weighted scores as an evaluated expression)
notes: Base unit 8.1. Students compare competing designs with a systematic process, such as a decision matrix that scores each design on each criterion and constraint, and choose the strongest. Completes MS-ETS1-2, started in s6-hazard-forecast and used in 7.2 and 7.6.

words: test data; compare; combine; redesign; best features
cross_subject: math:7.SP.B.4 (compare two data sets by center and spread)
notes: Base unit 8.1. Students analyze test results from several designs, find which features did best, and combine them into a new design that better meets the criteria. Completes MS-ETS1-3, used first in s7-design-optimize.

words: wave; vibration; amplitude; wavelength; frequency; pitch; medium; energy
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (describe a relationship from its graph)
notes: Base unit 8.2 (music from a truck shakes windows across a parking lot). Sound is a vibration passed through a medium by particles bumping their neighbours; it cannot cross empty space. A repeating wave is described by amplitude, wavelength and frequency; a larger amplitude carries more energy, which is why louder sound can shake a window. Students use graphs and simple numbers to relate amplitude and energy. Sound is also reflected, absorbed or transmitted by materials, the mechanical-wave half of MS-PS4-2 (owned by s6-light-paths, whose light model is reused). The wave-model, last used for signals in grade 6, is unused in grade 7 because the base text has no waves unit there. Boundary: no electromagnetic waves; standard repeating waves only. Teacher note: keep sound levels safe for hearing; no speakers held against ears. Assumes s6-light-paths across grade 7 (reflect, absorb, transmit now applied to sound); the base text has no waves unit in grade 7.

words: stimulus; receptor; signal; nerve; brain; response; memory; senses
cross_subject: ela:W.8.8 (gather and combine information from several sources)
notes: Base unit 8.2. Completes MS-LS1-8, built from 6.1 (light receptors), 6.6 (nerves carry signals), 7.1 (smell), 8.1 (touch, pressure, heat) and here (hearing). Students gather and combine information showing that each kind of receptor responds to its own input and sends signals to the brain, which turns them into an immediate action or a memory. Boundary: not how the signal travels along a nerve.

words: balanced; unbalanced; net force; mass; motion; reference frame; newton
cross_subject: math:7.NS.A.1 (net force as a sum of signed numbers)
notes: Base unit 8.3 (how a speaker moves without being touched), building on 8.1. Completes MS-PS2-2. Students plan investigations, changing one variable at a time, showing that an object's change in motion depends on the total of the forces on it and its mass: balanced forces leave motion unchanged, unbalanced forces change it, and the same force changes a smaller mass more. Forces are given in newtons and from a stated frame of reference. Boundary: one dimension; no trigonometry.

words: kinetic energy; speed; mass; relationship; graph; non-linear
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (qualitative features of a graph)
notes: Base units 8.1 and 8.3. Completes MS-PS3-1. Students build and read graphs showing that kinetic energy rises with mass and rises faster with speed (doubling speed far more than doubles the damage), keeping the two relationships separate. Carries the particle kinetic energy of grade 6 up to whole objects. Assumes s6-particle-temperature across grade 7: kinetic energy was met at the particle scale in grade 6, and grade 7 uses temperature but not the kinetic energy of whole objects.

words: energy transfer; kinetic energy; evidence; inventory; before and after
cross_subject: ela:W.8.1 (written argument)
notes: Base unit 8.3, drawing on 6.2 and 8.1. Completes MS-PS3-5. Students argue from evidence that whenever an object's kinetic energy changes (a cart slowing, a speaker cone moving, water warming), energy has been transferred to or from it, using a before and after energy inventory. Boundary: no energy calculations.

words: magnet; electromagnet; coil; current; electric force; magnetic force; strength
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.2 (is force proportional to the number of turns)
notes: Base unit 8.3. Students ask questions about data to find what makes electric and magnetic forces stronger: more coil turns or more current in an electromagnet, stronger or closer magnets, more charge. They use this to explain how a speaker's coil and magnet push the cone. Boundary: quantitative answers limited to proportional reasoning. Teacher note: strong magnets can pinch skin and harm devices; keep them away from pacemakers; coils from low-voltage batteries only, disconnected when warm.

words: field; non-contact force; charge; magnetic field; evidence; experimental design
notes: Base unit 8.3. Students investigate magnets, charged tape and charged balloons, and judge their own experimental design, to give evidence that a field exists between objects that push or pull without touching. Boundary: electric and magnetic fields only; qualitative evidence.

words: potential energy; stored energy; arrangement; distance; attract; repel
notes: Base unit 8.3. When two objects that interact at a distance are moved closer or farther apart, the energy stored in the system changes: lifting a book from the Earth, pulling magnets apart or bringing a charged balloon near hair. Students model the relative amounts. Boundary: two objects; electric, magnetic and gravitational; no calculation.

words: orbit; rotation; axis; tilt; lunar phase; eclipse; season; reflect
notes: Base unit 8.4 (patterns in the sky). Students build a physical and drawn model of the Earth, sun and moon to explain the cycle of moon phases (sunlight reflected from the half of the moon facing the sun), solar and lunar eclipses (shadows when the three line up), and seasons (the tilt of the Earth's axis, not distance from the sun). Reuses the grade 6 light-ray model and the earlier earth-sun-moon model; neither is used in grade 7 because the base text has no grade 7 unit on light or the sky. Also teaches the last elements of MS-PS4-2 (owned by s6-light-paths): light, unlike sound, crosses empty space, and colors bend by different amounts. Teacher note: never look at the sun directly or through a lens; eclipse viewing only through certified viewers or a pinhole projector. Assumes s6-light-paths across grade 7 because the base text places no light unit in grade 7.

words: gravity; gravitational force; mass; attract; distance; orbit
notes: Base unit 8.4. Students argue from data (simulations, tables of mass, distance and orbital period) that gravity always attracts and is stronger between larger masses. Boundary: no law of gravitation formula; no Kepler's laws.

words: solar system; galaxy; Milky Way; orbit; gravity; star
notes: Base unit 8.4. Gravity holds the solar system and the Milky Way together and controls the orbits within them. Students model orbits (physical or computer) and explain why planets keep circling instead of flying off or falling in. Boundary: no Kepler's laws.

words: scale; diameter; distance; astronomical unit; scale model; layer
cross_subject: math:8.EE.A.3 (powers of ten for very large numbers); math:7.G.A.1 (scale drawings)
notes: Base unit 8.4. Students analyze data on the sizes, distances and layers of objects in the solar system and build scale models showing how small the planets are against the distances between them. Boundary: no recall of facts about each planet.

words: gene; chromosome; protein; mutation; trait; allele; harmful; beneficial
notes: Base unit 8.5 (cattle with extra-large muscles). Genes on chromosomes carry the instructions for proteins; proteins build structures and do jobs that make traits. A change to a gene (a mutation) can change the protein and so the trait, with harmful, helpful or no effect on the organism. Builds on rearranging molecules in s7-cell-respiration-growth. Boundary: the chromosome and protein scale only; no DNA bases, no protein synthesis steps, no named kinds of mutation. The base text limits neutral effects to the idea, since evidence for them sits below this scale.

words: inherit; offspring; asexual; sexual reproduction; genetic variation; Punnett square; dominant; recessive
cross_subject: math:7.SP.C.8b (a Punnett square as a sample space for a compound event)
notes: Base unit 8.5. In asexual reproduction offspring get identical genetic information from one parent; in sexual reproduction each parent gives one of each pair of chromosomes, so offspring vary. Students use Punnett squares, diagrams and simulations to predict the chances of a trait. Teacher note: use animal and plant examples; never ask students to trace their own family's traits, which can expose adoption, donor conception or other private family facts.

words: nucleus; chloroplast; mitochondria; cell membrane; cell wall; organelle; function
notes: Base unit 8.5. Completes MS-LS1-2, built in 6.6 (membrane and wall), 7.4 (chloroplasts and mitochondria) and here (the nucleus holds the chromosomes). Students model the cell as a whole system and the role of each named part in it. Boundary: structure and function details only for the cell wall and membrane; the other parts only in relation to the whole cell; no biochemistry.

words: environment; genetic factor; growth; variable; drought; fertilizer
cross_subject: math:8.SP.A.1 (scatter plots of growth against a condition)
notes: Base unit 8.5, completing work begun in 7.3 (food and growth). Completes MS-LS1-5. Students explain from data how both genes and conditions (food, light, water, space) affect how large an organism grows: seed varieties in drought, fish in large and small ponds, cattle breeds. Boundary: no genetic mechanisms or biochemistry.

words: artificial selection; selective breeding; genetic engineering; gene therapy; technology; society
cross_subject: ela:W.8.8 (gather information from reliable sources)
notes: Base unit 8.5. Students gather and combine information from reliable sources on how people choose the traits of plants and animals (selective breeding, genetic modification) and treat genetic illness (gene therapy), and on the effects on society. Teacher note: questions of food and medicine choices are discussed as evidence and trade-offs; no student is asked to judge their own family's choices.

words: fossil record; extinction; diversity; rock layer; common ancestor; complexity
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-timeline-deep-time (deep-time timeline)
notes: Base unit 8.6 (a fossil of a giant ancient penguin). Students analyze fossils in rock layers for patterns: which life forms appear when, which go extinct, and how body structures change over time, assuming natural laws worked then as now. Builds on reading rock layers in s6-geologic-time. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5). Boundary: no names of individual species or geologic eras. Assumes s6-geologic-time across grade 7: the base text puts rock layers in 6.4 and the fossil record in 8.6, with no grade 7 unit between.

words: anatomy; similar structure; homologous; evolutionary relationship; ancestor
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students compare the gross anatomy of living and fossil organisms (flipper, wing and arm bones) to explain which are more closely related and share more recent common ancestors.

words: embryo; development; similarity; relatedness
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students compare pictures of embryos of different animals at matched stages to find similarities not seen in the adults, as further evidence of relatedness. Boundary: gross appearance only.

words: natural selection; variation; adaptation; survive; reproduce; environment; probability
cross_subject: math:7.SP.C.6 (probability from observed frequencies)
notes: Base unit 8.6. Individuals in a population vary; in a given environment some variations raise the chance of surviving and having offspring, so those traits become more common. Students explain this with probability statements and proportional reasoning. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5).

words: trait frequency; proportion; generation; increase; decrease; population change
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent change over generations)
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students use tables, graphs and simple simulations to show how the share of a trait in a population rises or falls over generations under natural selection. Boundary: no Hardy-Weinberg calculations.

words: courtship; pollination; pollinator; nectar; seed dispersal; reproduction; behavior
cross_subject: ela:W.8.1 (written argument)
notes: Base units 8.5 (flowers and pollinators) and 8.6 (animal behaviors). Completes MS-LS1-4. Students argue from evidence how animal behaviors (nest building, herding, calls and displays) and plant structures (bright flowers, nectar, hard shells) raise the chance of successful reproduction, including animals that help plants reproduce. Teacher note: reproduction is treated through plants and animal behavior, at the level of the standard.
